title: A leaking water pressure regulator means different things at the union, bell, bolt, and body
description: Mark the exact leak point, pressure condition, corrosion, and recent work before deciding whether sealing, service, or replacement is plausible.
prompt: Where does the first drop appear?
answer: A union leak can be an external connection problem; water from the bell, adjustment area, or body can point to a more serious valve condition. Trace the first wet point, not the lowest drip.
urgency: Active service-entry leakage can escalate quickly. Use the known whole-house emergency shutoff procedure and qualified help when flow cannot be contained.
diagramAlt: Pressure regulator with union, adjustment bolt, bell, and body leak points
identifiers: Union: first moisture appears at the connection face.
Bell or adjustment bolt: water emerges above the body.
Casting: a crack or porous corrosion wets the body itself.

choices.label: At a threaded or union connection
choices.detail: Connection alignment, seal, or corrosion may be involved.

choices.label: From the bell or adjustment bolt
choices.detail: Repeated adjustment is not a leak repair.

choices.label: Through a cracked or corroded body
choices.detail: Prepare for prompt replacement and safe isolation.

choices.label: The source may be above the valve
choices.detail: Dry and trace the first wet point before assigning the cause.

steps.title: Find the first wet point
steps.body: Dry the exterior and observe without disassembling a pressurized valve.

steps.title: Record pressure and severity
steps.body: Note static PSI, drip versus spray, and whether flow changes with fixtures.

steps.title: Choose connection repair or replacement scope
steps.body: Include isolation, fittings, setup, and related pressure checks.

safeChecks: Photograph corrosion and the leak origin.
notThisDevice: Condensation can mimic a slow exterior leak.
A leak above the regulator may track down the body.
An RPZ relief discharge uses a different safety path.
evidenceNote: Leak location is a routing clue. Depressurization and repair must follow the exact system and manufacturer procedure.
